title: Zero, First & Second Conditionals: Form and Use
grammarTitle: Zero, First & Second Conditionals — Form, Use & Subtle Differences
grammarNote: Три первых типа условных предложений охватывают всё: от универсальных фактов до гипотетических ситуаций. На уровне B1 важно не просто знать формулы, но понимать, почему выбирается тот или иной тип — какое отношение к реальности он выражает, и как тонкие изменения в выборе типа меняют смысл.

grammarTable.subject: ZERO conditional
grammarTable.example: "If water boils at 100°C." / "If she misses breakfast, she gets headaches."

grammarTable.subject: FIRST conditional
grammarTable.example: "If you study now, you will pass." / "If it rains, we'll cancel."

grammarTable.subject: SECOND conditional
grammarTable.example: "If I were you, I'd apply." / "If I had more time, I would help."

grammarTable.subject: Second: were to
grammarTable.verb: if + were to + base, would + base
grammarTable.example: "If the government were to raise taxes, inflation would fall." (formal)

grammarTable.subject: Unless
grammarTable.example: "Unless you study, you won't pass." = "If you don't study, you won't pass."

grammarTable.subject: Provided / As long as
grammarTable.example: "You can stay, provided you are quiet." / "...as long as you help."

grammarExtra.title: Zero vs First: certainty vs possibility

rows.example: "If you heat water to 100°C, it boils." (always — no exception) ✅
"If you heat the water, it will boil." (likely — you expect it to happen) ✅
Zero = law / fact. First = prediction / expectation. Same words, different relationship to reality.
"If you don't submit, you will fail." (warning) / "If you help me, I will return the favour." (promise) ✅

grammarExtra.title: First vs Second: real vs hypothetical

rows.form: First = the speaker thinks it's realistic
rows.example: "If I get the scholarship, I will go." (speaker expects this might happen) ✅

rows.form: Second = the speaker considers it unlikely or imagined
rows.example: "If I got the scholarship, I would go." (speaker doesn't really expect to get it) ✅
"If it rains, I'll cancel." (probable rain) vs "If it rained, I'd cancel." (unlikely — speaker expects sun) ✅
"If I were you, I'd apply." — hypothetical you, softer than "You should apply." ✅

grammarExtra.title: Second conditional: "were to" — formal and emphatic

rows.example: "If I were you, I'd reconsider." ✅ (NOT "If I was you" in formal English)
"If the government were to raise taxes, inflation would fall." — formal policy discussion ✅
"If she were to discover the truth, it would change everything." (emphasises: she won't, but suppose she did) ✅
"If I was richer, I'd travel more." — acceptable in informal/spoken English ✅

grammarExtra.title: Variations: unless / provided / as long as / in case

rows.example: "Unless you study, you won't pass." = "If you don't study, you won't pass." ✅

rows.form: PROVIDED (THAT) = only if the condition is met
rows.example: "You can stay, provided that you don't make noise." = "If you don't make noise, you can stay." ✅
"I'll help you, as long as you help me too." = same as "provided that." ✅

rows.form: IN CASE = because something might happen
rows.example: "Take an umbrella IN CASE it rains." (not IF) — preparing for a possibility, not stating a condition ✅

grammarExtra.title: ❌ Common errors with first and second conditionals

rows.form: ✗ "If I will go to Paris, I will visit the Eiffel Tower."
rows.example: ✅ "If I GO to Paris..." — if-clause uses Present Simple, NOT will! ✅

rows.form: ✗ "If I would have more time, I would help."
rows.example: ✅ "If I HAD more time, I would help." — if-clause uses Past Simple in 2nd conditional. ✅

rows.form: ✗ "If I was you, I would apply." (formal context)
rows.example: ✅ "If I WERE you..." — in formal English, always "were" not "was" for hypothetical. ✅

rows.form: ✗ "Unless you don't study, you won't pass."
rows.example: ✅ "Unless you study..." — "unless" already means "if not." Adding "don't" creates double negative. ✅

grammarTip:
Zero, First & Second Conditionals:

ZERO: if + PS, PS
→ Facts, laws, automatic results
"If water boils, steam rises."

FIRST: if + PS, will + base
→ Real possible future
"If you study, you WILL pass."
⚠️ NEVER "if you will study"

SECOND: if + Past Simple, would + base
→ Hypothetical / unlikely / imagined
"If I HAD more time, I WOULD help."
⚠️ NEVER "if I would have"

WERE TO = formal emphatic hypothetical:
"If I WERE TO apply, what would happen?"

Variations:
unless = if not
provided/as long as = only if
in case = preparing for possibility (≠ if)

💡 Real or hypothetical?
"If it rains, I'll cancel." → I think it might rain
"If it rained, I'd cancel." → I don't expect rain

exercises.text: "If you ___ this button, the screen ___." (automatic physical result)
exercises.hint: Automatic physical result = ZERO conditional. Present + Present. "If you PRESS this button, the screen TURNS OFF." ✅

exercises.instruction: First or Second? Choose based on meaning.
exercises.text: "___ I win this competition, I ___ spend the prize money on a trip." (speaker thinks winning is possible)
exercises.hint: Possible future (speaker thinks it could happen) = FIRST conditional. "If I win...I WILL spend..." ✅

exercises.text: "If I ___ (be) the university president, I ___ (make) tuition free."
exercises.hint: Second conditional: IF + WERE + would + base. "If I WERE the president, I WOULD MAKE tuition free." ✅ (NOT "was" in formal)

exercises.text: "If it will rain tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic."
opts: "will rain" should be "rains" — Present Simple in if-clause
exercises.correct: "will rain" should be "rains" — Present Simple in if-clause
exercises.hint: ✅ "If it RAINS tomorrow, we will cancel." — NEVER "will" in the if-clause of first conditional! ✅

exercises.text: Which is correct?
opts: "Unless you don't call, she won't know."
"Unless you will call, she won't know."
exercises.hint: "unless" = "if not" — already negative. "Unless you call" = "If you don't call." NEVER "unless you don't." ✅

exercises.text: "If the government ___ to reduce interest rates, inflation ___ fall."
exercises.hint: "were to" = formal emphatic hypothetical. "If the government WERE TO reduce rates, inflation WOULD fall." ✅

exercises.text: "You can borrow my notes, ___ you return them by Friday."
exercises.hint: "provided (that)" or "as long as" = only on the condition that. "You can borrow them PROVIDED you return them." ✅

exercises.text: "Take a spare pen ___ yours runs out during the exam."
exercises.hint: "IN CASE" = because something might happen (preparation). "Take a pen IN CASE yours runs out." ≠ "if" (which states a condition) ✅

exercises.text: "If I had a car, I would drive you to the station." — The speaker probably:
opts: is planning to buy a car
does NOT have a car — this is hypothetical
exercises.correct: does NOT have a car — this is hypothetical
exercises.hint: Second conditional = the speaker doesn't have a car. "If I HAD a car" = hypothetical (I don't). ✅

exercises.instruction: Change from first to second conditional to make hypothetical.
exercises.text: "If she applies, she will get the job." → Hypothetical: "If she ___ , she ___ get the job."
exercises.hint: 2nd conditional: "If she APPLIED, she WOULD get the job." (hypothetical — perhaps she won't apply or it's unlikely) ✅

exercises.instruction: Find the error in the second conditional.
exercises.text: "If I would have more time, I would study more languages."
opts: "would have" in if-clause is wrong — should be "had"
exercises.correct: "would have" in if-clause is wrong — should be "had"
exercises.hint: ✅ "If I HAD more time, I would study..." — if-clause uses PAST SIMPLE, never "would." ✅

exercises.instruction: Zero conditional for a scientific law.
exercises.text: "If you apply a force to a body, the body ___ according to F=ma."
exercises.hint: Scientific law = ZERO conditional. Present Simple both clauses. "the body ACCELERATES according to F=ma." ✅

exercises.text: Why do we say "If I were you" not "If I was you"?
opts: "Were" is the formal/subjunctive form required after "if" in hypothetical conditions (especially "if I were you")
exercises.correct: "Were" is the formal/subjunctive form required after "if" in hypothetical conditions (especially "if I were you")
exercises.hint: "If I were you" = subjunctive were = formal hypothetical. In formal/written English, always "were" not "was." ✅

exercises.text: "If you ___ (not finish) the report by 5, you ___ (miss) the deadline."
exercises.hint: First conditional warning: "If you DON'T FINISH... you WILL MISS..." Present Simple + will. ✅

exercises.text: "She looks exhausted. If she doesn't sleep now, ___ ."
exercises.hint: Real, likely consequence → First conditional. "If she doesn't sleep, she WILL FEEL worse tomorrow." ✅

exercises.text: "___ in your position, I would speak to the professor directly."
exercises.hint: "If I WERE in your position" — hypothetical you (I'm not in your position). Second conditional. "I WOULD speak..." ✅

exercises.text: "Whenever I ___ (feel) stressed, I ___ (go) for a run — it always helps."
exercises.hint: Habit/automatic response = ZERO conditional. Present + Present. "Whenever I FEEL stressed, I GO for a run." ✅

exercises.text: "If I ___ the president of Kazakhstan, I ___ invest more in rural education."
exercises.hint: Not realistic expectation = SECOND conditional. "If I WERE the president, I WOULD invest..." ✅

exercises.text: "If you leave now, ___ the 9 o'clock train." (realistic possibility)
exercises.hint: Realistic possibility + real train = FIRST conditional. "If you leave now, you'LL CATCH the 9 o'clock train." ✅

exercises.instruction: Identify: zero, first, or second conditional?
exercises.text: "If I spoke fluent Mandarin, I would have so many more job opportunities."
opts: Second — hypothetical (the speaker probably doesn't speak fluent Mandarin)
exercises.correct: Second — hypothetical (the speaker probably doesn't speak fluent Mandarin)
exercises.hint: if + Past Simple + would = SECOND conditional. Speaker probably doesn't speak fluent Mandarin. ✅

questions.hint: Zero conditional = certain, automatic results — laws, habits, facts. ✅

questions.text: "If you will study, you will pass." — What is wrong?
opts: "will study" in if-clause is wrong — should be "study" (Present Simple)
questions.correct: "will study" in if-clause is wrong — should be "study" (Present Simple)
questions.hint: ✅ "If you STUDY, you will pass." NEVER "will" in the if-clause. ✅

questions.text: Second conditional uses ___ in the if-clause.
questions.hint: Second conditional: if + PAST SIMPLE, would + base. "If I had more time, I would help." ✅
"unless" = "if not." "Unless you study" = "If you DON'T study." ✅
Second conditional: IF + WERE + would + base. "If I WERE taller, I WOULD PLAY professionally." ✅

questions.text: "If I were you" vs "If I was you" — in formal English:
questions.hint: "were" = subjunctive mood in hypothetical conditions. In formal English, always "If I WERE you." ✅

questions.text: "Take a first aid kit in case there is an accident." — "in case" means:
opts: Preparing for a possibility that might happen
questions.correct: Preparing for a possibility that might happen
questions.hint: "in case" = because X might happen — preparation, not a condition. "In case" ≠ "if." ✅

questions.text: "If it rains, I'll cancel." vs "If it rained, I'd cancel." — difference?
opts: First = speaker thinks rain is possible; Second = speaker doesn't expect rain
questions.correct: First = speaker thinks rain is possible; Second = speaker doesn't expect rain
questions.hint: First = realistic possibility. Second = hypothetical (speaker thinks it won't rain). Same event, different attitude. ✅

questions.text: "If the government were to introduce this law..." — "were to" is:
opts: Formal emphatic hypothetical — second conditional variant
questions.correct: Formal emphatic hypothetical — second conditional variant
questions.hint: "were to" = emphatic, formal second conditional. Stresses the hypothetical nature. ✅

opts: "If I would have time, I'd help."
"If I will have time, I'd help."
"If I had time, I will help."
questions.hint: "If I HAVE time, I'LL help." — First conditional. Present + will. ✅ All others have errors in if-clause.

questions.text: "Provided that you submit by Friday, I will accept it." — "provided that" means:
questions.hint: "provided that" = only on condition that. Similar to "if" but stronger emphasis on the condition. ✅

questions.text: The main difference between first and second conditional is:
opts: The speaker's view of likelihood — first = realistic, second = hypothetical/unlikely
questions.correct: The speaker's view of likelihood — first = realistic, second = hypothetical/unlikely
questions.hint: First = speaker considers it possible. Second = speaker considers it unlikely or imagined. ✅
